simple: a computer made of software, running on a real computer, that an operating system can use as if it were real.
analogy: the small school in the rented wing.
precise: an efficient, isolated duplicate of a real machine, in the words of Popek and Goldberg's definition: programs in it behave as on the real machine (equivalence), the monitor keeps control of the real resources (resource control), and most instructions run directly on the processor (efficiency).
source: D1, D2 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the program that creates virtual machines and stays in charge of the real hardware.
analogy: the large school's principal above the small school.
precise: the software that multiplexes the physical machine among virtual machines and handles the guest events it chooses to intercept; "type 1" hypervisors run on the hardware, "type 2" ones run as part of a host operating system (KVM makes the Linux kernel itself the hypervisor).
source: D2, D8 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the guest is the operating system inside the virtual machine; the host is the real machine and the software that runs the virtual machine.
analogy: the rented wing and the building that owns it.
precise: guest software runs with the virtual machine's view of the CPU, memory and devices; host software (the hypervisor and, for type 2, its host OS) owns the physical resources.
source: D2 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: an instruction whose effect depends on, or changes, who controls the machine.
analogy: touching the building's bell or master keys.
precise: an instruction that changes the processor's mode or the mapping of resources (control-sensitive) or whose result depends on them (behaviour-sensitive). Popek and Goldberg show that a machine can be virtualized by trap-and-emulate if every sensitive instruction is privileged.
source: D1 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: run the guest kernel with fewer rights; when it tries something only the real kernel may do, the processor stops it and the hypervisor does the job on its behalf.
analogy: the real principal steps in when the guest principal reaches for the real bell.
precise: deprivilege the guest kernel so that every privileged instruction traps to the monitor, which updates the virtual machine's state (a virtual interrupt flag, virtual control registers) and resumes the guest after the instruction.
source: D1, D2 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: rewrite the guest kernel's code on the fly so that the troublesome instructions are replaced before they run.
analogy: an assistant who reads the guest principal's notes before they are carried out and replaces "ring the bell" with "ask the real principal".
precise: the monitor translates guest kernel code into an instruction stream that is safe to run, emulating sensitive instructions in the translation; user-mode guest code runs directly. Early VMware used this on x86.
source: D3 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: change the guest operating system so that it asks the hypervisor directly instead of touching the hardware.
analogy: the guest principal is told about the arrangement and phones the real principal instead of reaching for the bell.
precise: a guest kernel ported to a virtual interface, using hypercalls and shared-memory devices instead of sensitive instructions and emulated hardware; early Xen required it for x86 guests.
source: D4 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a call from the guest kernel to the hypervisor.
analogy: the phone line from the guest principal's desk to the real principal.
precise: a deliberate transfer of control from guest to hypervisor with arguments in registers, the virtual-machine counterpart of a system call (VMCALL on Intel VMX, VMMCALL on AMD SVM, HVC on Arm).
source: D6, D7 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: processor features that let a guest kernel run at its usual privilege level while the hypervisor still catches what it must.
analogy: the building gives the small school its own copy of the office, and an alarm on the few doors that matter.
precise: a new processor mode for guests (VMX non-root operation on Intel, guest mode under SVM on AMD, EL1 under EL2 on Arm, VS mode under HS mode on RISC-V), a per-virtual-CPU control structure (VMCS, VMCB) that says which events to intercept, and VM exits and entries between guest and hypervisor.
source: D6, D7, C1 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: an exit is the moment the guest is stopped and the hypervisor runs; an entry is the moment the guest resumes.
analogy: the real principal stepping in, and stepping out again.
precise: a VM exit saves the guest's processor state in the control structure, loads the hypervisor's, and records the reason (exit reason on VMX, exit code on SVM) and qualifying details; a VM entry (VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME, VMRUN) does the reverse after checking the guest state.
source: D6, D7, D10 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: what the guest believes is a real memory address.
analogy: the room numbers on the small school's own floor plan, which the building translates to its real rooms.
precise: the address produced by the guest's own page tables; the hypervisor translates it to a host-physical address, in software (shadow page tables) or with nested paging.
source: D2, D5 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a second set of page tables, owned by the hypervisor, that the processor walks after the guest's own tables.
analogy: the building's master plan, consulted after the small school's floor plan.
precise: hardware translation of guest-physical to host-physical addresses through hypervisor-controlled tables (Intel extended page tables, AMD nested page tables, Arm stage-2 translation, RISC-V G-stage translation), which makes every guest page-table access itself a translated access: a two-dimensional walk.
source: D5, C1 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)
related: Nested page table (NPT) and nested CR3

simple: page tables that the hypervisor builds by combining the guest's tables with its own, before nested paging existed.
analogy: the building's clerk keeps a merged copy of the small school's plan, with real room numbers, and must update it every time the school changes its plan.
precise: monitor-maintained tables mapping guest-virtual directly to host-physical addresses, kept consistent by write-protecting guest page tables and trapping changes and CR3 loads.
source: D2, D3 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a hypervisor running inside a virtual machine, with its own guests.
analogy: the small school rents part of its wing to a third, even smaller school.
precise: running a hypervisor as a guest, with the outer hypervisor emulating the virtualization extensions for it; the usual way to develop a hypervisor (DR404's labs run theirs under QEMU's emulation instead).
source: D9, C1 of F4-38 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a bit that a hypervisor sets in the CPU's self-description to say "you are in a virtual machine".
analogy: the door plate that says "Wing B, property of the main school".
precise: bit 31 of ECX returned by CPUID leaf 1; real processors return 0 there, and hypervisors that want to be found return 1 and then answer the leaf range starting at 0x40000000.
source: D1, R1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a 12-character name returned by the CPU instruction that describes the processor, when the hypervisor answers it.
analogy: the name of the building's owner on the plate.
precise: the bytes of EBX, ECX and EDX returned by CPUID leaf 0x40000000, for example "KVMKVMKVM" followed by zero bytes for KVM and "TCGTCGTCGTCG" for QEMU without acceleration; EAX gives the highest hypervisor leaf.
source: D2, R1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a clock the hypervisor keeps up to date in the guest's memory, so the guest can read the time without asking.
analogy: the building's master clock, with a repeater in each wing.
precise: a per-virtual-CPU record (TSC value, system time at that value, a multiplier and shift to convert TSC ticks to nanoseconds, a version counter) that the guest registers through KVM-specific MSRs; the guest computes the time from the record and the TSC.
source: D3, C1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a counter that the writer makes odd while it changes a record and even when it is done, so a reader can tell whether what it read was half-changed.
analogy: a "being updated" sign hung on the timetable board while the secretary rewrites it.
precise: a reader copies the version, the fields, then the version again, and retries if the version was odd or changed; the writer increments the version before and after the update.
source: D3, R6 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: time when the guest's virtual CPU wanted to run but the host ran something else.
analogy: lesson time lost because the main school borrowed the room.
precise: a per-vCPU counter the hypervisor publishes (KVM's steal-time feature) so the guest's scheduler and accounting can tell real idle time from time taken away.
source: D3, C1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a change in a guest OS that makes it aware of, and cooperate with, its hypervisor.
analogy: the guest principal reading the building's rules and following them.
precise: the use of paravirtual interfaces (clocks, end-of-interrupt shortcuts, TLB-flush hypercalls, synthetic timers) instead of emulated hardware; "Hyper-V enlightenments" is the name used for Hyper-V's set.
source: C1, D4 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a device through which the host asks the guest to give back memory it is not using.
analogy: the guest school returning empty classrooms so the building can lend them elsewhere.
precise: virtio-balloon: the guest driver allocates pages ("inflates") and tells the host their addresses, which the host can then reclaim.
source: D5, C1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a socket connection between a guest and its host that needs no network set-up.
analogy: an internal phone line between the wing and the main office.
precise: the virtio-vsock device and its socket address family, addressing endpoints by context ID and port.
source: D5, C1 of F4-39 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: AMD's processor extension for running virtual machines.
analogy: the building's rule book that lets a second school run inside it.
precise: Secure Virtual Machine: enabled by EFER.SVME; adds VMRUN, VMLOAD, VMSAVE, VMMCALL, STGI, CLGI and the VMCB; guest-mode execution ends in #VMEXIT with an exit code.
source: D1, C1 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: Intel's extension for the same purpose.
analogy: another building's rule book, with different forms.
precise: Virtual Machine Extensions: VMXON enters root operation; VMLAUNCH and VMRESUME enter non-root operation with a VMCS selected by VMPTRLD and accessed by VMREAD and VMWRITE.
source: D2, C1 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: one page of memory that describes a virtual CPU to the processor.
analogy: the written agreement and the small school's state, on one sheet.
precise: virtual machine control block: a 4 KiB, page-aligned structure with a control area (intercepts, I/O and MSR bitmap addresses, ASID, exit code and information, event injection, nested paging) and a state-save area (segments, control registers, EFER, RIP, RSP, RAX and more).
source: D1 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: Intel's counterpart of the VMCB.
analogy: the same agreement on the other building's forms, which only the clerk may read and write.
precise: virtual machine control structure, accessed only through VMREAD and VMWRITE with field encodings; its layout in memory is not architectural.
source: D2 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a rule saying "this event must stop the guest and call the hypervisor".
analogy: "call me when you touch the bell".
precise: a control bit in the VMCB (or an execution control in the VMCS) that turns an instruction, register access, exception or interrupt in guest mode into a VM exit.
source: D1, D2 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a table with one bit per I/O port, saying which ports the guest may not touch directly.
analogy: the list of doors with an alarm.
precise: on SVM, a physically contiguous bitmap whose address is in the VMCB; a set bit makes IN or OUT to that port exit with code IOIO when the IOIO intercept is on.
source: D1 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the number that says why the guest stopped, and the details that go with it.
analogy: the line in the ledger: "rang the bell, east wing, 10:42".
precise: on SVM, EXITCODE in the VMCB (names from SVM_EXIT_*: 0x7B IOIO, 0x72 CPUID, 0x78 HLT, 0x7F SHUTDOWN, 0x81 VMMCALL, 0x400 NPF, −1 ERR) with EXITINFO1 and EXITINFO2; on VMX, the exit reason (basic reason in bits 15:0) and the exit qualification.
source: D3, R6 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the processor refuses to start the guest because its described state breaks a rule.
analogy: the agreement is not signed properly, so the small school is not let in.
precise: on SVM, VMRUN performs consistency checks and on failure exits immediately with EXITCODE = −1 (SVM_EXIT_ERR, "invalid_guest_state" in Linux's table); on VMX, VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME either fail as an instruction (with a VM-instruction error number) or the entry fails after loading and exits with bit 31 of the exit reason set (basic reason 33 for invalid guest state).
source: D3, D2, R3 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a number tagging the guest's TLB entries so they are not mixed with the host's.
analogy: a coloured sticker on every key copy, one colour per school.
precise: address space identifier in the VMCB; ASID 0 belongs to the host, and VMRUN rejects it for a guest. Intel's equivalent is the VPID.
source: D1, R3 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: an extra on/off switch for interrupts, above the usual one, used while switching between host and guest.
analogy: the real principal's "do not disturb" sign during the hand-over.
precise: an SVM flag cleared by CLGI and set by STGI; while it is clear, interrupts are held pending, so the hypervisor can enter and leave the guest atomically.
source: D1 of F4-40 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

term: Nested page table (NPT) and nested CR3
simple: the hypervisor's page table that says where each guest "physical" page really is.
analogy: the building's master plan for the guest school's rooms.
precise: on AMD SVM, enabled by the VMCB's NP_ENABLE bit; its root is N_CR3, a host-physical address; entries use the long-mode page-table format and translate guest-physical to host-physical addresses for every guest memory access, including the guest's own page-table reads. Intel's equivalent is EPT, rooted at the EPT pointer.
source: D1, D2 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)
related: Nested page fault (NPF) and EPT violation

term: Nested page fault (NPF) and EPT violation
simple: the exit that happens when the guest touches guest-physical memory the hypervisor's table does not allow.
analogy: the guest school walks to "room 3000", which does not exist on the building's plan, and the real principal is called.
precise: SVM exit code 0x400 (SVM_EXIT_NPF) with the guest-physical address in EXITINFO2 and an error code in EXITINFO1; on VMX, basic exit reason 48 (EPT violation) with the address in a VMCS field and the access type in the exit qualification.
source: D3, R5 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)
related: Nested page table (NPT) and nested CR3

simple: the hypervisor makes the guest receive an interrupt or exception as if hardware had raised it.
analogy: the real principal rings the small school's bell for them.
precise: on SVM, writing a vector, a type (external interrupt, exception, software interrupt) and a valid bit into the VMCB's EVENTINJ field; the processor delivers the event through the guest's IDT at the next VMRUN. VMX uses the VM-entry interruption-information field.
source: D1, R2 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the hypervisor's imitation of the chip that hands interrupts to the processor.
analogy: the small school's own bell board, run by the real principal.
precise: a software model of an interrupt controller (here, the 8259 PIC's initialisation words, mask and end-of-interrupt) that decides when an injected interrupt is allowed; hardware assistance (APIC virtualization, AVIC, GICv4) moves part of this into the processor.
source: C1 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the memory the guest believes is its RAM, starting at address 0.
analogy: the guest school's rooms, numbered from 1 on its own plan.
precise: the address space produced by the guest's page tables and translated by the nested table; in the lab, guest-physical 0–32 MiB is one host buffer at host-physical 0x600000.
source: R1 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)
related: Nested page table (NPT) and nested CR3

simple: timer interrupts the guest should have received but did not, because it was not running at the time.
analogy: bells that rang while the small school's staff were out of the building.
precise: when a periodic virtual timer comes due while the vCPU is not running or cannot take interrupts, the hypervisor must either deliver the missed ticks later (catch-up) or drop them; either choice distorts a guest that counts ticks to measure time.
source: D4, R3 of F4-41 (D = documents, title only unless the chapter says they were opened in this build, dossier gate G1 open; C1 = curriculum map; R = lab runs in this build)
